opus-5.5.text:
Jeff is a pretty remarkable person to have as an advisor, and I think a lot of people at Google Brain would say the same.

The first thing that stands out is his technical depth and breadth. He's one of those rare people who can go from talking about low-level systems details, like how you lay out memory or parallelize a computation across thousands of machines, all the way up to the research question of what model architecture or training objective makes sense. When you bring him a problem, he often sees the bottleneck very quickly, whether it's a modeling issue or an infrastructure issue. For research at scale, that combination matters a lot.

The second thing is that he's very generous with his time and very encouraging. Given how senior he is, you might expect him to be hard to reach or only interested in the big picture. But he engages with the details of what you're doing, and he's genuinely enthusiastic about ideas, even early, half-baked ones. That makes people feel comfortable trying ambitious things.

Third, he has very good intuition about where things are going. Early on at Brain, a lot of people outside were skeptical that just scaling up neural networks with more data and more compute would keep paying off. Jeff believed in that direction early and pushed the organization to build the infrastructure to make it possible. As a researcher, having an advisor who is willing to bet on long-term directions, and who gives you the resources and air cover to pursue them, is incredibly valuable.

And he's very humble and low-ego for someone of his stature. He doesn't make it about himself. He cares about the work getting done and about the people doing it growing. A lot of the culture at Brain, the openness, the bottom-up research, the freedom to publish and explore, reflected his style.

If I had to point to anything, it's that he's so fast and has so many ideas that you need to filter and prioritize, because he'll suggest ten interesting directions and you can only pursue one or two. But that's a good problem to have. Overall, I'd say he's one of the best advisors you could ask for, especially if you want to do research that combines strong engineering with ambitious scientific goals.

fable-5.1.text:
Working with Jeff was honestly one of the formative experiences of my career, so let me try to be concrete rather than just gushing.

The first thing that strikes you is the bandwidth. Jeff could sit in a meeting on, say, a language model experiment, and within a few minutes he'd have done the back-of-the-envelope math on how many FLOPs you were burning, where the bottleneck in the pipeline was, and whether the idea could scale ten or a hundred times. He carries this almost physical intuition for systems: latency numbers, memory bandwidth, how many bytes are moving through the network. So when he advised you, the advice was never abstract. It was "this won't work because of this specific constraint, and here's how you might get around it."

The second thing is that he gave people enormous room. He didn't micromanage. He'd ask a few sharp questions, point you toward someone who had solved a related problem, and then let you go. For me, especially early on, that trust was a little terrifying, but it was also what made me grow. You learned to own your own research direction because he expected you to.

He was also remarkably generous with credit and with his time. I'd send him a draft at an odd hour and get thoughtful comments back surprisingly quickly, sometimes line by line. And he genuinely cared whether the work mattered, not just whether it would make a nice paper. He'd push on "who is this going to help, and how do we get it into a product or into other people's hands?"

If I had to name a weakness, it's that his optimism and speed can set a bar that's hard for normal humans to match. You'd leave a conversation energized and also slightly worried you weren't thinking big enough. But that's a pretty good problem to have in an advisor. Overall, he shaped how I think about research: start with the scale and the systems, ask what's actually useful, and give the people around you room to run.

He also gives you room to develop your own ideas. That balance of guidance and independence is what I appreciate.
